To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hypoxia and inhibition of metabolism inhibit Na+/Ca2+.
hypoxia and inhibition of metabolism slow the increase in [free calcium] induced by reverse-mode Na+/ca2+ exchange in cardiac myocytes.
hypoxia and inhibition of glycolysis inhibit Na+/Ca2+-exchange and the processes that lead to Ca2+ release.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Na+/Ca2+-exchange in the pathogenesis of cardiac myocyte damage.
the role of the sodium-calcium exchanger in the pathophysiology of ischemia.
the role of the sarcolemal Na+/Ca2+-exchanger in the pathogenesis of cardiac arrhythmia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Na+/Ca2+-exchange activity of cardiac myocytes was reduced by hypoxia and by metabolic inhibition.
hypoxia and inhibition of glycolysis inhibit reverse-mode Na+/ Ca2+ exchange.
the Na+/Ca2+-exchange system in cardiac myocytes is sensitive to hypoxia.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypoxia and/or metabolic inhibition inhibit the reverse mode of Na+/Ca2+, the Na+/Ca2+-activated Ca2+ release, and the Na+-independent Ca2+ influx.
hypoxia and Na+/H+ exchange inhibition cause a decrease in the rate of Na+ influx, which in turn leads to a decline in Ca2+ influx through Na+/Ca2+.
Na+/Ca2+-exchange in the sarcolemma of cardiac myocytes is inhibited by hypoxia and by metabolic inhibition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypoxia and the inhibition of glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation cause a significant decline in reverse-mode Na+/ Ca2+ exchange in cardiac myocytes.
hypoxia and inhibition of oxidative phosphorylation inhibit Na+/Ca2+-exchange in cardiac myocytes.
Na+/Ca2+-exchange is a major mechanism of Ca2+ entry in cardiac cells.
